<reason>CON kept the debate anchored on the motion's actual clause—"even if response times increase"—and forced PRO to defend the wait rather than the clinician. CON's pressure questions extracted a concrete dispatch rule from PRO ("suicidal talk without a weapon" goes to the slow team) and an admission that there is no minute ceiling, then used both to show the delay lands precisely where it is most lethal. CON's answer to PRO's questions ("fast default, not armed default," via co-response and crisis-trained patrol) dissolved much of PRO's badge-versus-clock framing. PRO's best live route—the parent who never calls because police will come—was real and well-stated, and CON never fully refuted it, but CON's weighing (the caller already on the line vs. a hypothesized non-caller) was more persuasive to a third party. PRO also partly narrowed "mental health calls" by carving out overdoses and ledges, which CON correctly noted cannot be sorted before arrival. CON's clipped final rebuttal is a minor execution cost but the substance landed before the cut. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5–B4.7: CON took PRO's own dispatch rule from A4.1 ("suicidal talk without a weapon" gets the slower team) and PRO's admissions that the stacked delay is "a real cost" with no minute cap, and showed the motion routes its uncapped delay to the calls where a locked bathroom door decides survival—turning PRO's honest answers into the case against the motion.</best_rebuttal>
